criterion_notes.c1: Examines community and household drinking-water supply and aqueduct service access in the Bribri Indigenous community of Amubri (and neighbouring Cachabri and Suiri sharing the aqueduct) in Talamanca, Costa Rica, from 1990 to 2022.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it analyzes public water policies, institutional interventions by the national water utility (AyA) and Ministry of Health, and Indigenous community water governance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it empirically examines concrete regulatory, administrative, documentation, and cost-recovery rules directly governing service access and sustainability: (1) tariff and cost-recovery rules requiring delegated community aqueducts (ASADAS) to self-finance operations strictly through user tariffs without State operational subsidies, alongside local flat-rate tariff rules (2,000 colones/month without metering, and Suiri residents refusing to pay above 500 colones and splitting off into a separate committee); (2) administrative reporting and legal-personality documentation requirements, whereby missing financial reports place the aqueduct in the lowest category (Category C) of AyA's SAGA system and the lack of legal personality (personería jurídica) under differentiated Indigenous territorial norms restricts backing for public funds, donations, and piping materials; and (3) delegated utility regulatory structure (AyA/ASADAS) and Ministry of Health sanitary orders (órdenes sanitarias) and chlorination mandates.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-historical and interpretive empirical case study (approved by the University of Costa Rica Scientific Ethics Committee, linked to UCR research project B9314) triangulating primary institutional files (AyA Expediente 7-4-4 Amubri-Cachabri-Suiri from 1990-2020 and Ministry of Health records), qualitative interviews with institutional officials and Indigenous residents, transcripts of two community workshops, field visits, and 2019/2021 microbiological water-quality laboratory analyses (INISA). Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for systematic-review mechanism synthesis regardless of lacking quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household/subscriber connection coverage over time (230-254 households in 1990s-2003; 244 households in Amubri, 160 in Suiri, 80 in Cachabri, and 4 schools without meters in 2011-2012; 650 subscribers covering ~2,265 residents in 2022), tariff affordability and payment compliance/conflicts (2,000 vs. 500 colones flat monthly fees, financial insufficiency for maintenance/disinfection), seasonal water availability/stream drying, and service potability/continuity failures.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies population and units of analysis (community aqueduct system and subscriber households in the Bribri Indigenous community of Amubri and connected communities Cachabri and Suiri, Talamanca, Costa Rica), legal/institutional exposures, service access/sustainability/affordability/quality outcomes, and qualitative socio-historical case-study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish (with bilingual Spanish/English abstract). Per Criterion 10, Spanish is eligible because full-text translation is directly feasible and this empirical study provides important socio-legal mechanism evidence on Indigenous community aqueduct governance, legal-personality documentation barriers, and tariff cost-recovery rules; translation method and translator must be logged in extraction_note during extraction.

evidence_quotes.quote: Durante este periodo, el acueducto abastecía a 244 hogares en Amubri, 160 en Suiri, 80 en Cachabri, y cuatro centros educativos, todos sin medidores.

Al 2022, el acueducto de estudio contaba con 650 abonados (cubriendo una población aproximada de 2265 personas) que cancelan una cuota mensual de 2000 colones (equivalente a aproximadamente 4 USD al tipo de cambio promedio de 2025). Sin embargo, esta tarifa resulta insuficiente para la sostenibilidad y funcionamiento óptimo de las condiciones del acueducto.

Según indicó, la comunidad no quiere colocar medidores y tampoco subir la tarifa plana que cobran, lo que dificulta en la práctica a las personas del comité poder hacer las mejorar realmente necesarias y dar mantenimientos adecuados (desinfectar, comprar insumos y poder asegurar y pagarle al fontanero que debe ser calificado). Sumado a esto, la funcionaria indicó que ellos conocen el conflicto entre Suiri y las otras comunidades del acueducto, pero indican que el conflicto se basa en que en esa comunidad los abonados no quieren pagar más de 500 colones, mientras el resto de los abonados de las otras comunidades pagan 2000 colones

Lo anterior, sumado a la falta de información financiera que debería brindar la administración del acueducto al AyA, hace que el acueducto que abastece la comunidad sea catalogado por el Sistema de Apoyo y Gestión de ASADAS (SAGA) en categoría C (categoría más baja). Aunque reconoció que la institución ha hecho un esfuerzo para cambiar el sistema y categorizar de forma separada a las comunidades indígenas debido a que presentan situaciones atípicas, tales como normativas diferenciadas y falta de personerías jurídicas que permitan respaldar “el manejo de fondos públicos, donaciones, todo eso de tuberías y cosas de ese tipo”

Las fuentes primarias incluyen expedientes institucionales del Instituto Costarricense de Acueductos y Alcantarillados (AyA) que compila el trabajo de sus diferentes unidades estratégica de negocios (UEN) y del Ministerio de Salud, informes técnicos, análisis de calidad del agua, normativa, registros de giras de campo, transcripciones de dos talleres comunitarios y entrevistas cualitativas realizadas a actores clave, tanto institucionales como comunitarios.

raw_response.exposure: Delegated community water utility regulatory framework (AyA / ASADAS), mandatory tariff-only cost-recovery rules without State operational subsidy (flat monthly fees vs. metering), SAGA administrative/financial reporting classification (Category C) and legal-personality (personería jurídica) documentation requirements for receiving public funds/donations/piping materials in Indigenous territories, and Ministry of Health sanitary orders and chlorination mandates.
raw_response.outcome: Household/subscriber aqueduct connections (reaching 650 subscribers / ~2,265 people by 2022), tariff affordability and payment compliance/disputes (2,000 vs. 500 colones monthly flat fee; Suiri committee split over non-payment), financial/operational sustainability of aqueduct maintenance, seasonal water availability, and drinking-water potability.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Bribri Indigenous community of Amubri (alongside neighbouring Cachabri and Suiri sharing the aqueduct; 650 subscribers / ~2,265 residents in 2022) in the Talamanca Bribri Indigenous Territory, Limón province, Costa Rica; primary data include AyA archival expediente 7-4-4 (1990-2020), qualitative interviews with institutional officials and community members, two community workshops, and 2019/2021 INISA water samples (units of analysis: community aqueduct / water committee and subscriber households).
raw_response.rationale: This qualitative socio-historical empirical case study (1990-2022) meets all systematic-review inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Beyond general water governance, it empirically documents specific legal, administrative, and cost-recovery rules governing Indigenous community drinking-water access and service sustainability in Amubri, Costa Rica: (1) strict tariff-based cost-recovery rules without State subsidy for delegated community aqueducts (ASADAS), flat-tariff and non-metering rules, and inter-community tariff disputes (2,000 vs. 500 colones) driving committee fragmentation; (2) SAGA administrative/financial reporting rules (Category C rating) and lack of legal personality (personería jurídica) under differentiated Indigenous territorial norms, which impede access to public funds, donations, and piping materials; and (3) sanitary orders and chlorination regulations. Full text in Spanish is directly translatable per Criterion 10, and qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for mechanism synthesis.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative socio-historical and interpretive empirical case study (combining archival institutional records, qualitative interviews, two community workshops, field observations, and microbiological water-quality testing, 1990-2022)
